query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid SPS processing combined with mechanical alloying induces a metastable microstructure in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs that is enriched in Ti. Upon high-temperature exposure, this metastable state transforms via Ti segregation to form a continuous, thin TiO2 passivation layer that markedly improves both corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, metastable microstructure with a uniform elemental distribution but subtle Ti enrichment achieved via rapid SPS and mechanical alloying.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 600°C in air) and chloride-containing corrosion testing (e.g., 0.1 M NaCl solution) while comparing to a conventionally processed, equilibrium microstructure.
generation.conditions: Lightweight HEA with density below 6 g/cm3, processed via rapid SPS combined with mechanical alloying versus a conventional slow-sintered control, then subjected to high-temperature (≥500°C) and corrosive (0.1 M NaCl) environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and growth of Ti-rich precipitates that coalesce into a coherent TiO2 film on the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: The rapid SPS and mechanical alloying suppress grain growth and generate a metastable state with a latent Ti enrichment. Upon high-temperature exposure, thermally activated diffusion leads to Ti segregation and nucleation of Ti-rich phases which transform into a protective TiO2 layer. This layer acts as a self-passivating barrier, limiting further oxygen ingress and metal ion dissolution during corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-sintered metastable baseline, the alloy will exhibit lower corrosion current densities and reduced oxidation weight gain, corresponding to the presence of a continuous TiO2 passivation film.
generation.baseline: The as-sintered metastable alloy state prior to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion exposure, which lacks a fully developed TiO2 passivation layer.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected only for alloys processed by rapid SPS combined with mechanical alloying; alloys processed by conventional slow sintering, which yield more equilibrium microstructures, may not exhibit the same degree of Ti segregation or passivation.
generation.uncertainty: The kinetics of Ti segregation, the uniformity of the resulting TiO2 film, and the precise dependency of corrosion/oxidation resistance improvements on film continuity require further characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples: one processed via rapid SPS with mechanical alloying and one processed by conventional slow sintering. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 600°C in air for a fixed duration) and electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., immersion in 0.1 M NaCl with potentiodynamic polarization).
measurements: Characterize surface compositions and the presence of a TiO2 passivation layer using XPS and TEM
Measure oxide weight gain during high-temperature exposure
Determine corrosion current densities from electrochemical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid SPS processed samples do not show a significantly thicker or more continuous TiO2 film, and if their corrosion current density and oxide weight gain are not measurably lower than those of the conventionally processed controls, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. In the present study, the optimal spark plasma sintering (SPS) parameters for the investigated alloy were established based on systematic experiments, in which material density and microstructural stability were adopted as the main criteria. Sintering tests were performed over a temperature range of 875–1100 °C in 25 °C increments, under a constant punch pressure of 50 MPa. The experimental results indicate that at 50 MPa, the most favorable sintering temperature was 1050 °C, yielding a nearly fully dense material with minimal porosity. These findings further confirm the high efficiency of the SPS technique, allowing for the fabrication of dense solids at relatively low temperatures and significantly reduced processing times. Additionally, the rapid densification and short exposure to elevated temperatures effectively limited grain growth in the resulting material []. reading.lever: Combine rapid SPS processing with mechanical alloying to induce a metastable microstructure enriched in Ti for self-passivation.
reading.why: This combined processing method leverages established SPS densification and Ti-driven passivation from Mg–Ti–Zn systems, potentially revealing transformation pathways affecting corrosion and oxidation in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs.
